extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment based on quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems under point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may use internal control or a conformity assessment involving a notified body depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications were applied.

Annex VII (notified body route) is required/mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI systems, while most other high-risk AI systems not embedded in regulated products under Annex I can use the internal control (self-assessment) route under Annex VI.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Under Article 43, for the purposes of the conformity assessment procedure in Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except that where the system is to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or EU institutions/bodies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to authorise, by derogation from Article 43, the placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system for a limited period, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, without the normal conformity assessment.

Annex VII section 4.5 provides that a notified body may, where necessary and after other reasonable means have been exhausted, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

Article 44 covers certificates issued by notified bodies, Article 45 covers information obligations of notified bodies, Article 47 covers the EU declaration of conformity, and Article 48 covers CE marking, as part of Section 5 (Standards, Conformity Assessment, Certificates, Registration) of the AI Act.
Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes the administrative framework for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies.

As of March 2026, no AI Act notified bodies had yet completed designation; the notified body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across member states and limited capacity.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act.

A September 2026 proposal (COM(2025) 836 / 2025/0359 COD) would add a new Annex XIV listing codes and categories of AI systems for the Commission's NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) information system, to register AI Act notified bodies.

A Council document (7322/26) sets out proposed AIP codes (e.g., AIP 0101-0105) corresponding to categories of AI systems under Annex I for scoping the designation of conformity assessment bodies under Article 30.

Post-2026, notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments, with the intersection with MDR/IVDR notified body assessments still being worked out.

The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) rules on notified bodies started applying 11 June 2026; as of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated for the CRA in NANDO, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026 and full CRA application from 11 December 2027.

As of October 2025, NANDO lists 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies (under the Medical Devices Regulation and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation), separate from AI Act designations.
The European Commission publishes a list of designated notified bodies in the NANDO information system, searchable by legislation.

High-risk AI obligations under the AI Act were originally set to fully apply from 2 December 2027 (for Annex III systems), but the date has reportedly been extended, in a final text agreed in September 2026, to 2 August 2029.

The extension of the Annex III high-risk deadline to 2 August 2029 was reportedly made because harmonised standards and notified bodies are not yet ready; until then, providers reportedly do not need a conformity assessment by a notified body for Annex III systems.

One source states that August 2026 is 'the key deadline' for high-risk AI obligations to fully apply, including for medical device AI/SaMD, with notified bodies designated under the AI Act expected to begin assessments afterward; another source refers to an 'August 2026 deadline' for engaging a notified body as not moving.

A step-by-step guide notes that the European Commission may update the Annex VI and Annex VII conformity assessment procedures via delegated acts under Article 43(5) and Article 97, without needing to revise the AI Act itself.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act and the Status of Notified Body Designations

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control and notified-body assessment — with the applicable route depending on the type of system and whether harmonised standards exist (low confidence). As of the most recent sources (March–September 2026), no notified bodies had yet been formally designated under the AI Act, and the infrastructure for designation (NANDO listings, Annex XIV codes) remains under development (low confidence). Separately, the deadline for full application of high-risk obligations is contested across sources: while the September 2026 reports of an extension to 2 August 2029 each individually score as high-confidence under the scoring methodology, the central timeline question remains genuinely uncertain because these reports contradict earlier sources citing August 2026 or December 2027, and no official adopted text confirms which date currently governs.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment based on a quality management system and technical documentation review by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric identification systems under point 1 of Annex III, providers may use internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some sources interpret the notified-body route as effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk systems eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by sectoral EU harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery) listed in Annex I Section A, providers must follow existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Providers may generally choose any notified body, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs the role (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits derogation from standard conformity assessment for limited periods on exceptional public security, health, or infrastructure grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Annex VII also allows notified bodies, under safeguards, access to training data and model parameters to verify compliance (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Related provisions cover certificates (Article 44), notified body information duties (Article 45), the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), and CE marking (Article 48) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Article 35 establishes the administrative framework for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35)). As of March and April 2026, no AI Act notified bodies had been formally designated, with designation processes still ongoing across member states (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A September 2026 legislative proposal (COM(2025) 836) would add a new Annex XIV to support NANDO registration of AI Act notified bodies, with associated "AIP" codes proposed for scoping designations under Article 30 (medium confidence) ([Council document ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [COM(2025) 836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). ## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control and notified-body assessment — with the applicable route depending on the type of system and whether harmonised standards exist (low confidence). As of the most recent sources (March–September 2026), no notified bodies had yet been formally designated under the AI Act, and the infrastructure for designation (NANDO listings, Annex XIV codes) remains under development (low confidence), while the deadline for full application of high-risk obligations is itself contested across sources, ranging from August 2026 to December 2027 to a reported extension to August 2029.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment based on a quality management system and technical documentation review by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric identification systems under point 1 of Annex III, providers may use internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some sources interpret the notified-body route as effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, with most other high-risk systems eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by sectoral EU harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery) listed in Annex I Section A, providers must follow existing sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications generally trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)).
